query_snapshot: What does NBS Circular 592 report about the corrosion behavior of stainless steels in sulfuric acid at approximately 150 degrees Fahrenheit across acid concentrations, and how should that affect a screening conclusion?
final_answer:
Evidence-grounded answer:

- Kiefer and Renshaw reported that molybdenum-bearing types 316 and 317 were the most resistant to sulfuric acid at low temperatures. [nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- NBS Circular 592 states that at about 150°F all of the stainless steels corrode in practically all concentrations of sulfuric acid from [UNREADABLE lower bound] to 95 percent. [nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- Roach and Hall reported that molybdenum-bearing stainless steels were useful at room temperature in sulfuric acid concentrations below 15 percent and above 85 percent. [nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- The Circular reports that resistance to sulfuric acid is improved in some cases by additions of copper or cerium. [nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- NBS Circular 592 describes Hastelloy A as usefully resistant to sulfuric acid of all concentrations at temperatures up to about 160°F (presented as an example of a higher-resistance alloy). [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 79-80, chunk 6745f7b0]
- Inference — For screening, do not conclude that stainless steel is acceptable for sulfuric-acid service at ≈150°F across concentrations; require alloy-, temperature-, and concentration-specific corrosion-rate data or select a more resistant alloy. [nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1; nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 79-80, chunk 6745f7b0]
